title: Let the lender pace a key's traffic and absorb a throttle, and let tests inject provider faults through it
foundBy: session agent operating two eight-member campaigns side by side on one host, reading every member's own CLI session records and the lender containers' logs after both campaigns had ended
details:
**The observation behind it.** Eight members of two campaigns shared one provider key whose limit was 500,000 input tokens a minute. Their combined demand, summed from their own session records, had a median of 483,000 a minute for the whole of both campaigns. Cached input was counted toward the limit in full. One member with a large context was enough to reach the ceiling by itself. An agent loop makes a request every ten seconds or so and each re-sends the whole context, so 145,000 tokens six times a minute is 870,000. Every member had to discover the limit separately, by failing. The members with the largest requests were the ones that lost the contention every time. Each failure cost a turn and, in a campaign, a recovery ladder that added to the load (the campaign ledger's SAC-034).

**The idea.** No member can see the total. The lender can: every call on a key already passes through it. It could hold a per-slot budget and **queue** a request that would exceed it rather than forward it. When the provider throttles anyway, it could **wait the provider's retry-after and try again** instead of returning the 429. A CLI would then see latency and never a rate limit, for every CLI family at once. Two fleets on one key would become a queue rather than a fight. The budget has to be configured rather than guessed, because limits differ by key and tier. A stall watchdog downstream has to be able to tell a queued request from a wedged one, so queueing must be visible (SBX-046).

**The caution.** The proxy's present virtue is that it never reads a body: *"a stream passes through byte for byte and a request shape this build has never seen still works."* Pacing by tokens needs a size. The request's byte length is a usable proxy for it and keeps that property; parsing the body would not.

**The second half, which is cheaper and may be worth doing first.** Because every call passes through the lender, it is also where provider faults can be **injected** for tests. It could answer the next N calls on a slot with 429, with 503, with a hang, with a 401. That gives this repository and the campaign repository a way to prove what a turn driver, a wrapper and a recovery ladder do under each fault. It needs a throwaway sandbox and not a real campaign. Every behaviour in SBX-044, SBX-045, SAC-034 and SAC-035 was learned from two four-hour campaigns because nothing cheaper could produce the condition.

notes.text: The `details` text was copy-edited so the repository's prose gate passes: long sentences were split and em-dashes removed, and no claim was changed. The text as filed is in commit c059533.

This was measured while fixing the retry budget in SBX-045. Codex 0.152.1 never retries an HTTP 429 status, whatever its retry counts say. It retries only a rate limit delivered inside the response stream. A provider or gateway that throttles with a bare 429 ends a codex turn at once, and the lender is the only place that can absorb it.
